source.title: Fact Finding: Attempting to Reverse-Engineer Factual Recall on the Neuron Level (Post 1)

record.tranche_reason: The post discusses superposition and reports a neuron-level finding, but it does not test any listed version: its reported mixed activations are described as sport-related, not as responses to unrelated inputs.
record.gate_note: The post reports one Pythia neuron that is not monosemantic on a broader data distribution, but does not establish unrelated activations or estimate how common such neurons are. Other discussion of superposition is background or speculation; cited results from other work are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: The post studies factual recall circuitry in Pythia 2.8B. Its only neuron-level polysemanticity observation is a qualitative remark that one neuron (L5N6045) is 'not monosemantic' on broader data. It does not say the extra activations are unrelated inputs, does not quantify prevalence across neurons or layers, and does not test causes, architecture effects or measurement dependence. Superposition is invoked as background and speculation, not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is right. Early MLPs (2-6) in Pythia 2.8B act as multi-token embeddings producing linearly recoverable attributes, and the internal lookup mechanism appears uninterpretable. Single-step detokenization and strong hash-and-lookup are falsified. Superposition is treated as important but poorly understood.
record.recipe_differences: The post does not apply the original neuron visualization or measurement method to test the listed claims.

fits_no_version.finding: Baseball neuron L5N6045 in Pythia 2.8B often fires on sport-related text outside athlete names but is called not monosemantic; no unrelated categories are reported.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Task-relevant neurons in LM MLPs found by circuit analysis are often not monosemantic on the broader data distribution.

record.problems: The neuron-level finding is qualitative and concerns one neuron; the post does not quantify prevalence or show that its activation categories are unrelated. The authors also note that their main analysis studied 1,500 facts while the five MLP layers each had 10,000 neurons.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant neuron-response results were reported. The neuron’s cosine similarity to a baseball direction and its causal connection to a fact-extracting head concern its role in the circuit, not whether it responds to unrelated inputs.

untested.parts: All parts; no vision models are studied.
Share of polysemantic MLP neurons and layer variation; only one neuron is mentioned qualitatively.
Superposition as cause; it is asserted as background, with SAE success cited as evidence, but not tested.
Whether mixtures reduce to a shared feature. The sport-related description hints at this but is not tested.

record.verdict_notes: The post defines polysemanticity in a footnote ('fires on multiple unrelated things') and claims, without numbers, that distributed representations are qualitatively more common in language than image models. This is speculation, not a result, so it gets no row. The study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: The post studies Pythia 2.8B, but does not report a large share of MLP neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts, or compare prevalence across layers.
It discusses superposition as a possible explanation, but does not test whether polysemanticity is caused by representing more sparse features than there are neurons.
It does not test polysemanticity arising from initialization, regularization, or training noise without capacity pressure.
It does not compare activation functions, architectures, or regularization effects on polysemanticity.

The reported neuron is described as activating on sport-related things; the post does not test whether canonical unrelated mixtures resolve to a shared feature or whether truly unrelated mixtures are rare.
It does not compare ways of examining activation ranges or scoring explanations.

rows.subject: Pythia 2.8B, L5N6045
rows.operation_detail: Measured neuron activation on athlete names.
rows.value: Activated significantly more on the names of baseball-playing athletes.
rows.locator: Post 3 Summary, Hash and lookup hypothesis
rows.note: The result distinguishes baseball-player names from other players, but does not report unrelated input categories.
rows.check: This is a selectivity result for a baseball neuron within the task. It is not a polysemanticity measurement, and it is arguably evidence of sport selectivity rather than a row on any version.

rows.subject: Pythia 2.8B, L5N6045
rows.operation_detail: Measured activation on a broader data distribution.

conditions.value: broader data distribution than athlete names

rows.value: Often activates on sport-related things, but is not monosemantic.
rows.locator: Post 3 Summary, Hash and lookup hypothesis
rows.note: The text explicitly calls the neuron not monosemantic, while describing its broader activations as sport-related; it does not establish unrelated mixtures.
rows.check: One neuron is described qualitatively as not monosemantic but often sport-related. No unrelated categories are named and no prevalence is given, so it cannot bear on V2's 'large share' claim. No number is reported.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
